The Cinnamon flycatcher (Pyrrhomyias cinnamomeus) is a small passerine inhabiting montane cloud forests of the Andes, whose life history traits remain comparatively little studied despite its broad distribution. Recent field measurements have begun to illuminate the energetic foundations of its life cycle. Under controlled conditions that match the body temperature typical of active individuals, 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C], basal metabolic rate was recorded at 36.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour [JOi = 36.36 milliliters of oxygen per hour], a value that provides the benchmark for understanding daily energy requirements in this species. This resting oxygen consumption reflects the relatively modest metabolic demands of a bird of this size, though it is notably higher than values reported for some tyrant flycatchers of comparable mass from warmer lowland habitats. The initial mass of the freshly laid egg, measured soon after oviposition before significant water loss occurs, averages approximately 2.41 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.41 grams], representing a considerable parental investment given the adult female body size. This egg mass is consistent with the altricial development pattern typical of suboscine passerines, where the energy-rich yolk supports rapid embryo growth during the incubation period that follows.

A more detailed understanding of the early developmental trajectory emerges from studies of nestling growth in the wild. Incubation experiments conducted under controlled thermal conditions reveal that at a constant temperature of 34 °C [T = 34 °C], embryos complete development and hatch after exactly 14 days [ab = 14 days], a duration that aligns closely with the incubation periods documented for several other Andean tyrannids with similar egg masses. Upon hatching, the neonate weighs just 1.5 grams [Wwb = 1.5 grams], an extremely low birth mass that underscores the altricial nature of the chicks and their complete dependence on parental provisioning for thermoregulation and feeding. This hatchling mass represents only a fraction of the ultimate adult body size, setting the stage for a period of extraordinarily rapid mass gain during the nestling phase. The contrast between the small neonate and the fully grown adult highlights the intensity of parental care required during the early weeks of life, a period during which both parents make frequent foraging trips to deliver insects and other arthropod prey to the constantly begging nestlings.

Fledging, defined as the achievement of sustained flight capability and departure from the nest, occurs at 15 days after hatching [tx = 15 days after hatching], a relatively brief nestling period that is characteristic of many Neotropical insectivorous passerines facing high predation risk in open-cup nesting sites at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This early fledging age places considerable demands on the post-fledging parental care period, as the young birds remain dependent on adults for food and protection for several additional weeks. Sexual maturity, or the onset of gonadal maturation, follows a longer developmental trajectory, with puberty attained at 45 days after hatching [tp = 45 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40.2 °C [T = 40.2 °C]. This timing suggests that individuals reach reproductive capability during the same breeding season in which they hatched, though actual first breeding attempts may be deferred until the following year depending on resource availability and social competition for territories within the dense cloud forest understory.

Females typically lay 4 to 6 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 4 to 6 eggs per clutch], a modest clutch size that is typical for tropical montane passerines where the pace of life is slower and per-capita investment in each offspring is higher. The frequency of nesting attempts is similarly constrained, with pairs producing between 1 and 2 clutches per year [F_R_i = between 1 and 2 clutches per year], depending on the length of the favorable season and the success of the initial brood. This relatively low annual fecundity is balanced by an extended lifespan, which allows multiple breeding opportunities across the adult years. The time since birth at first successful reproduction, marking the age when a female produces her first brood, is approximately 1.3 years [tR = approximately 1.3 years], a delay that reflects the time required to establish a territory, find a mate, and complete the necessary gonadal and behavioral maturation before initiating the first clutch of the reproductive career.
